by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and the asset is being tested under §§ 33-1101, 33-1123, or 33-1125.
by_task.procedure: Treat statutory dollar limits as protection ceilings, not eligibility tests: a firearm may qualify under § 33-1125(10) and a motor vehicle under § 33-1125(8) even when its value exceeds the limit. Assess each listed vehicle independently. Use § 33-1125(4) only for engagement or wedding rings and § 33-1125(1) only for wearing apparel.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not extend the ring exemption to other jewelry, do not classify jewelry as apparel, and do not list administrative rules such as §§ 33-1101(B), 33-1121, or 33-1133(B) as asset exemptions.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and an asset satisfies the stated property category.
by_task.procedure: For each independent alternative, claim no more than the asset value and the applicable ceiling: $15,000 for a motor vehicle, $2,000 aggregate for firearms, and $2,000 aggregate for engagement and wedding rings. A qualifying over-limit asset remains eligible at the capped amount.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not award the ring ceiling to bracelets, necklaces, pendants, or other jewelry, and do not add administrative provisions as separate claim alternatives.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and the asset actually is a listed § 522(d)(3) household furnishing, household good, wearing-apparel item, appliance, book, animal, crop, or musical instrument.
by_task.procedure: Report the independent § 522(d)(3) alternative at the lesser of the asset value and $700 for that particular item; do not double this item ceiling for joint debtors.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use § 522(d)(3) for jewelry or firearms, and do not recast a musical instrument as a § 522(d)(6) tool of the trade without facts showing trade use.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and an asset is tested under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(3) or (d)(4).
by_task.procedure: Use § 522(d)(3) for listed household goods, furnishings, apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, or musical instruments, and § 522(d)(4) for jewelry. A value above the applicable ceiling does not defeat eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry or firearms under § 522(d)(3), and do not omit a qualifying category merely because the asset exceeds its dollar limit.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are an allowable namespace and the asset is property of the estate.
by_task.procedure: After checking the asset-specific paragraphs, independently add 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) for every asset because it covers any property. Before finalizing, check each asset separately and retain this alternative even when a specific Federal or state exemption also applies. A dollar ceiling limits value, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not add it when Federal exemptions are not allowable, and do not treat 11 U.S.C. §§ 522(b), 522(d), or 522(m) as asset exemptions.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and valuing the independent 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) alternative.
by_task.procedure: Always report § 522(d)(5) separately for every asset, including an asset also eligible under § 522(d)(1) or another specific paragraph. Unless the facts state that § 522(d)(1) has actually consumed an amount, claim the lesser of asset value and $15,425 per debtor; for equally owned joint property, cap each half separately, allowing up to $30,850 total.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit the wildcard because a specific exemption applies, do not use only the $1,475 base when no actual homestead consumption is stated, and do not use it outside the Federal namespace.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property used personally rather than for business.
by_task.procedure: Add 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) as an independent alternative for any such property, including property also covered by a specific subsection. Add subsection (a) only for necessary wearing apparel, Bibles, school books, or family pictures, and subsection (e) only for professionally prescribed health aids.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not exclude an asset from subsection (b) merely because it is jewelry, a vehicle, household property, or a health aid; do not call jewelry wearing apparel.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and valuing independently applicable personal-property alternatives.
by_task.procedure: For subsection (b), report the lesser of asset value and $4,000 for one debtor; for equally owned property of two debtors, cap each half separately, allowing up to $8,000 total. Separately report subsection (c) at no more than $2,400 for a motor vehicle, and report qualifying subsection (a) wearing apparel or subsection (e) prescribed health aids at the asset value because those supplied provisions state no dollar ceiling.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the subsection (b) ceiling for a specific subsection, report zero-value alternatives, double the $2,400 vehicle ceiling, or infer business use solely from words such as business, work, or toolbox in an item's name.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and valuing a qualifying rifle, shotgun, or pistol.
by_task.procedure: Report the lesser of asset value and $1,000 under § 18.362, and separately report the lesser of asset value and $400 under § 18.345(1)(p).
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the $1,000 firearm ceiling for the $400 personal-property alternative, and do not double either amount merely because there are joint debtors.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: In addition to every applicable specific Oregon category, independently add Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) for each item of personal property, including a vehicle, firearm, household item, apparel, jewelry, or prescribed health aid. Treat apparel and jewelry under § 18.345(1)(b), and household goods or furnishings under § 18.345(1)(f). A value above $400 does not defeat § 18.345(1)(p) eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 18.345(1)(p) to real property or a homestead, and do not classify clothing or jewelry as household furnishings merely because it is used personally.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and valuing the independent § 18.345(1)(p) alternative.
by_task.procedure: Report the lesser of the asset value and $400 for § 18.345(1)(p), independently of any specific Oregon exemption and independently for each asset.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not increase this reported alternative merely because there are joint debtors, and do not apply it to real property.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the debtor has an interest in the asset.
by_task.procedure: Add 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent alternative for every kind of property, including real property and business or personal property. Check every asset separately even when another Federal or Pennsylvania exemption applies. Its $300 ceiling limits protection, not eligibility. Separately add § 8124(a) subsections only when the asset actually is wearing apparel, a Bible or school book, a qualifying sewing machine, or a qualifying military uniform or accoutrement.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not withhold § 8123 because the asset exceeds $300 or lacks a listed § 8124 category; do not classify firearms, jewelry, household linens, or vehicles as wearing apparel, and do not cite § 8124(a) without a qualifying subsection.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and valuing the independent § 8123 alternative.
by_task.procedure: Claim the lesser of the asset value and $300 for one debtor; because each married spouse is entitled to the exemption, use up to $600 for jointly owned property of two debtors.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not transfer § 8124 category rules to unrelated property or use Pennsylvania amounts when that namespace is not allowable.
